subject: Biology
title: Gene Regulation
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Gene Regulation.

hook.text: Every cell in your body has the same DNA, yet a skin cell looks nothing like a neuron.

buildup.text: The difference is which genes are turned on. Cells activate only the genes they need.

discovery.text: Proteins called transcription factors bind DNA and switch genes on or off.

twist.text: A liver cell and a muscle cell read entirely different chapters of the same genetic book.

climax.text: Gene regulation explains how one genome builds over 200 different cell types.

punchline.text: Same book, different chapters. That's regulation.

quiz.question: Why do different cell types look and act differently despite having the same DNA?

details.summary: Gene regulation controls when, where, and how much a gene is expressed. Cells use promoters, enhancers, transcription factors, and epigenetic modifications to fine-tune gene activity, ensuring proper development and response to environmental signals.
details.whyItMatters: Regulation is why a skin cell behaves differently from a brain cell despite having identical DNA. Errors in gene regulation cause cancers, developmental disorders, and autoimmune diseases, making it central to medicine.
takeaways: Transcription factors bind DNA to activate or repress specific genes
Enhancers can regulate genes from thousands of base pairs away
Cells constantly adjust gene expression in response to signals

faq.question: How do transcription factors know which genes to activate?
faq.answer: Transcription factors have DNA-binding domains that recognize specific short sequences near genes. When a signal activates the transcription factor, it binds its target sequences and recruits RNA polymerase to begin transcribing the gene.

faq.question: What happens when gene regulation goes wrong?
faq.answer: Misregulation can cause cells to grow uncontrollably leading to cancer, to differentiate incorrectly causing developmental defects, or to produce harmful immune responses in autoimmune disease. Many diseases are fundamentally regulation problems, not gene defects.
